questions.source: LC Biology HL 2014, Section C, Question 11 (c)
questions.stem: Read the following extract and then answer the questions below. Alzheimer's disease (a degenerative brain condition), like many other degenerative illnesses, is driven by genes and recently scientists have identified a group of genes that are thought to be associated with this disease. The disease is thought to be caused by a build up of protein-based plaques in the brain, and investigators now believe they have an understanding of ways to interrupt that process. Technology is helping too, as researchers exploit new ways to scan the brain and detect the first signs of trouble, peering deeper into human and animal neural tissue to pinpoint the very molecules that give rise to the disease. (Adapted from Alzheimer's Unlocked, TIME, Volume 176, No. 17. 2010.)

parts.label: (v)
parts.text: How is the advance of technology helping in the fight against the disease?

points.answer: Scans can examine the brain (for early detection)

parts.label: (vi)
parts.text: There are probably more people suffering from the disease now than ever before. Suggest a reason for this.

points.answer: Larger population or more people living into old age

points.answer: 1. Cornea: allows light in or refracts light

3. Eustachian tube: equalise pressure (between the middle ear and the outside)

questions.stem: For each of the following structures, identify its precise location and its main function.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: Cerebellum. Precise location: ... Main function: ...

points.answer: Precise location: back of the brain
Main function: coordination (control) of muscular movement or balance or posture or walking or writing or fine muscle movements or speech

questions.source: LC Biology HL 2026, Section C, Question 17 (d)
questions.stem: The human nervous system can be divided into two main parts – the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS contains the brain and the spinal cord. Electrical impulses are carried through these systems by neurons. The diagram shows a section through the spinal cord.

diagram.what: Grey drawing of a transverse section of the spinal cord: a pale outer region round a darker butterfly-shaped inner region, with a tiny central canal in the middle ('Central canal'); P points to the pale outer region near the top, Q to the darker inner region, and Y to the thin covering round the outside at the bottom right.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Name the fluid found in the central canal.
parts.scheme_note: * in scheme = a specific term is required; a correct answer is cancelled if an incorrect answer is added.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: 1. Name the protective tissue Y surrounding the spinal cord that has three layers. 2. Name one other structure that protects the spinal cord.
parts.scheme_note: * in scheme = a specific term is required; a correct answer is cancelled if an incorrect answer is added.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: Name the regions of the spinal cord labelled P and Q.
parts.scheme_note: * in scheme = a specific term is required; a correct answer is cancelled if an incorrect answer is added.

parts.label: (iv) 1.
parts.text: 1. Draw a large diagram of a neuron.

points.answer: Diagram: dendrites and cell body with a nucleus and axon

parts.scheme_note: One missing = 3 marks; two missing = 0 marks.

parts.label: (iv) 2.
parts.text: 2. On your diagram label the following parts: Axon; Dendrite; Myelin sheath

parts.label: (iv) 3.
parts.text: 3. On your diagram indicate with an arrow the direction of travel of an impulse.

points.answer: Arrow from dendrite towards axon or away from the cell body

parts.label: (v)
parts.text: Describe the mechanism of a reflex action.

points.answer: Receptor detects stimulus or impulse (or message) generated (at receptor)
Passes to an interneuron or to the CNS (or grey matter)
Passes to the effector or effector reacts or muscle contracts

parts.scheme_note: If 'impulse' or 'message' is not mentioned, award a maximum of 2(3).

questions.source: SEC Sample Paper 1 (2027), Higher Level, Question 1 (b)
questions.stem: The diagram shows a synapse in the nervous system.

diagram.what: Coloured diagram of a synapse: the swollen end of one neuron (below, orange outline) holding round vesicles with dots inside; across a gap above it, the membrane of the next neuron with Y-shaped receptors; small dots of chemical in the gap. A points to one of the dots in the gap; B to a vesicle in the lower neuron.

parts.label: (i)
parts.text: Molecule A and structure B have roles in neurotransmission. Identify A and B.
parts.scheme_note: Unofficial: SimpleStudy practice marking scheme for the SEC sample paper (not an SEC document); the marks are its indicative allocation. The scheme accepts a named neurotransmitter, such as acetylcholine.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.text: On the diagram on the right, draw an arrow to show the direction the nerve impulse is transferred.

points.answer: An arrow drawn pointing from the lower structure containing the vesicles towards the upper membrane carrying the receptors (upwards in the printed diagram, from the presynaptic neuron across the cleft to the postsynaptic membrane)

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial: SimpleStudy practice marking scheme for the SEC sample paper (not an SEC document); the marks are its indicative allocation.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.text: What happens to the molecules labelled A after the nerve impulse transmission is complete?

points.answer: It is broken down by an enzyme in the synaptic cleft, for example acetylcholinesterase breaking down acetylcholine
The products are reabsorbed into the presynaptic neuron and used to resynthesise the transmitter

parts.scheme_note: Unofficial: SimpleStudy practice marking scheme for the SEC sample paper (not an SEC document); the marks are its indicative allocation. The essential point either way is that the transmitter is removed, so that the postsynaptic neuron is not stimulated continuously.

not_covered: Dopamine and endorphins: their roles in mood and behaviour, and how lifestyle choices (non-medical drug use, exercise, diet) change their levels (2.4.9) - never asked; dopamine appears only as 'lack of dopamine' in the cause of Parkinson's disease.

Drugs that work at the synapse: enzyme inhibitors that stop a neurotransmitter being broken down, reuptake inhibitors, psychoactive drugs and painkillers, and the enhanced effect they create (2.4.8) - only 2004-Q15a(iii) (a drug may inhibit or enhance transmission).

Acute and chronic disorders caused by disruptions to synaptic transmission, as a group (2.4.8) - questions ask only for the cause and treatment of Parkinson's disease or paralysis (and Alzheimer's, 2014-Q11c).

Homeostasis as stimulus-response by negative feedback, with a control centre linking receptors and effectors (2.4.5) - never asked of the nervous system; only 2004-Q12c(iv) (the responses to a fall in body temperature). Hormonal feedback is in the endocrine chapter.

The peripheral nervous system: where its nerve fibres and cell bodies lie (ganglia, dorsal and ventral roots) (2.4.4) - only the scheme's 'and ganglia' (2025-Q14a) and the reflex-arc arrows in and out of the cord (2010-Q11b).
Modelling impulse travel across a synaptic cleft (2.4.8) - no question asks for a model.
